n: As one of his first acts as king, David consults all his military leaders. He wants the whole nation involved in his plan.
David proposes gathering all Israel, including priests and Levites, but only “if it be of the LORD.” He seeks both the people’s agreement and God’s will.

f.w: that it be of the LORD our God

n: His goal: bring back the ark of the covenant, which had been neglected during Saul’s reign. For the chronicler, restoring true worship is the first priority of a good king.

f.g: The sacred chest holding the tablets of the law, symbol of God’s presence.

f.w: we inquired not at it in the days of Saul

n: Everyone agrees—the plan seems right to all the people.

f.w: the thing was right in the eyes of all the people
f.g: Popular agreement, though as the story shows, method matters as well as motive.

n: David gathers Israel from its southern border with Egypt to Hamath in the far north to bring the ark from Kirjath-jearim, where it had rested for about twenty years or more.

f.g: A stream or branch of the Nile region marking Israel’s southwest border.

n: The ark is called by the Lord’s name, the One enthroned between the cherubim. It represented God’s throne on earth.
They place the ark on a new cart—the way the Philistines had moved it—rather than having Levites carry it on poles as God’s law required.
David and all Israel celebrate wholeheartedly with music and song. Their joy is real—but their method is still wrong.

f.g: Stringed instruments like small harps or lyres.

n: At a threshing floor the oxen stumble, and Uzza reaches out to steady the ark.

f.g: Called Nachon’s threshing floor in 2 Samuel 6:6.

n: God strikes Uzza dead for touching the ark. The law warned that even Levites who handled the holy objects improperly would die. It is a sobering lesson that God’s holy things must be approached His way. Latter-day scripture uses “steadying the ark” as an image for trying to correct God’s work without authority.

f.w: he put his hand to the ark

n: David is upset that the Lord “broke out” against Uzza. The place is named Perez-uzza, “the breaking out against Uzza.”

f.g: Angry or distressed; perhaps both grief and frustration.

n: David becomes afraid of God and wonders how he can ever bring the ark home. Reverent fear leads him, in time, to learn the right way.
Instead of bringing it into Jerusalem, David leaves the ark at the house of Obed-edom.

f.g: Possibly from Gath-rimmon, a Levite town; he later appears among the Levite gatekeepers (1 Chronicles 26:4).

n: During the three months the ark stays there, the Lord richly blesses Obed-edom’s household. The same holy presence that brought death to the careless brought blessing to the reverent.

f.w: the LORD blessed the house of Obed-edom
